nodes.name: Poisson integral of boundary data
nodes.statement:
Boundary data is a vector measure $
u$ with values in a real normed space, and \[ P[
u](w)=\int P_w(z)\,d
u(z). \] The kernel is real-valued, so it pairs with $
u$ by scalar multiplication. A finite positive measure $\mu$ enters as the associated signed measure, and data given as a function $f$ against a reference measure $\mu$ enters as the vector measure $f\,d\mu$. For a finite positive measure, compatibility with the ordinary integral gives $P[\mu](w)=\int P_w\,d\mu$ for every $w$, without a support hypothesis. This follows from the integral pairing identity for the associated signed measure.
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: def:poisson_integral

nodes.name: Basic properties of the Poisson integral
nodes.statement:
For vector measures, $P[-
u]=-P[
u]$ and $P[a
u]=aP[
u]$ for $a\in\mathbb R$. If $P_w$ is integrable against $|
u_1|$ and $|
u_2|$, then $P[
u_1\pm
u_2](w)=P[
u_1](w)\pm P[
u_2](w)$. Let $w\in\mathbb{D}(c,R)$, let $\mu$ be a finite positive measure carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}(c,R)$, and let $k\in L^1(\mu)$ be real. The kernel $P_w$ is integrable against $\mu$ and the variation of $k\,d\mu$, and \[ P[k\,d\mu](w)=\int P_w(z)k(z)\,d\mu(z). \] For a finite signed measure $
u$ carried by the same circle, $P_w$ is integrable against $|
u|$ and its Jordan decomposition gives \[ P[
u](w)=\int P_w\,d
u^+-\int P_w\,d
u^-. \] Differences of finite positive measures carried by the circle are still carried by the circle, and their Poisson integrals subtract accordingly. For a positive measure, $P[\mu](w)\ge0$.  egin{proof} Linearity follows from the vector-measure integral. At an interior point the kernel is bounded on the boundary circle, which gives the stated integrability. Split a real density into its positive and negative parts to obtain the density formula. Apply linearity to the Jordan decomposition to obtain the signed-measure formula. Positivity follows from $P_w\ge0$ on the boundary circle. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:poisson_integral_linear

nodes.name: Poisson integrals of boundary data are harmonic
nodes.statement: For a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by the circle and real $k\in L^1(\mu)$, both $P[\mu]$ and $P[k\,d\mu]$ are harmonic inside. If $f$ is continuous on $\partial\mathbb{D}(c,R)$ then $P[f\,d\sigma]$ is harmonic on the open disc, where $\sigma$ is normalized arclength. \begin{proof} For a positive measure, take the real part of its analytic Herglotz--Riesz transform. For a real density, split it into its positive and negative parts and use linearity. Harmonicity of the circle average follows from harmonicity of the kernel in the interior variable, by differentiating under the integral sign. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:harmonic_poisson_integral

nodes.name: Poisson integral formula
nodes.statement: If $u$ is harmonic on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\mathbb{D}}(c,R)$ then $u(w)=P[u\,d\sigma_{c,R}](w)$ for every interior $w$. Taking $u\equiv 1$ gives $P[\sigma_{c,R}](w)=1$: the kernel has total mass one at every interior point. \begin{proof} Transport to the circle average and apply the mathlib form of the Poisson formula. Total mass one is the case $u\equiv 1$, read through the density lemma. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:poisson_reproducing

nodes.name: Dirichlet problem on a disc
nodes.statement: For continuous real boundary data $u$ on $\partial\mathbb{D}(c,R)$ there is a function continuous on $\overline{\mathbb{D}}(c,R)$, harmonic inside, equal to $P[u\,d\sigma_{c,R}]$ on the open disc and to $u$ on the circle. \begin{proof} The Poisson kernel has mass one and its mass away from a boundary point tends uniformly to zero. Uniform continuity of the boundary data gives continuity of the extension; interior harmonicity is already formalized. The continuous-extension declaration still has an open proof. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:poisson_extension

nodes.name: A boundary measure is determined by its Poisson integral
nodes.statement:
\mainline  ookref{Garnett}{I.3, after Theorem 3.1}{Printed page 15, PDF page 27} If $\mu$ and $
u$ are finite signed measures carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}(c,R)$, $R>0$, with $P[\mu]=P[
u]$ on $\mathbb{D}(c,R)$, then $\mu=
u$.  egin{proof} The standard weak-star argument: $P[\mu](r\,\cdot)\,d\sigma	o\mu$ when tested against continuous functions on the circle, because the Poisson integral of continuous data converges uniformly to it. This is what licenses speaking of \emph{the} representing measure in Theorem~ef{thm:II_5_3}, and it is used again in the uniqueness part of the canonical factorization (Theorem~ef{thm:nevanlinna_factorization_uniqueness}) and in Garnett's Theorem II.5.4. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:poisson_measure_unique

nodes.name: Nontangential approach region
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.4}{Chapter I, Section 4, printed page 21, PDF page 33, disc form} For $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb{D}$ and $\alpha>1$ put \[ \Gamma_\alpha(\zeta) =\Bigl\{z\in\mathbb{D}:\ |\zeta-z|<\alpha\,(1-|z|)\Bigr\}, \] a teardrop-shaped region asymptotic at $\zeta$ to an angle with vertex $\zeta$. Facts to record: $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$ is open and contained in $\mathbb{D}$; it increases with $\alpha$; it contains the radial segment $[0,1)\zeta$; it is empty when $\alpha\le 1$; and $\Gamma_\alpha(1)$ is mathlib's \texttt{Complex.stolzSet}~$\alpha$, with $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)=\zeta\cdot\Gamma_\alpha(1)$. Mathlib only has the region at $\zeta=1$, so the rotated family has to be added.
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: def:nt_region

nodes.name: Nontangential limit
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.5}{Chapter I, Section 5, printed page 27, PDF page 39} Write $\mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta)$ for the neighbourhood filter of $\zeta$ within $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$. The \emph{nontangential filter} at $\zeta$ is their supremum in the lattice of filters, \[ \mathcal{N}_\zeta=\sup_{\alpha>1}\ \mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta). \] For $\alpha>1$, $f$ has limit $L$ at $\zeta$ \emph{within} $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$ if $f\to L$ along $\mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta)$, and $f$ has \emph{nontangential limit} $L$ at $\zeta$ if $f\to L$ along $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$. The two are related by \[ f\to L \ \text{along}\ \mathcal{N}_\zeta \iff \forall\,\alpha>1,\ f\to L \ \text{along}\ \mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta). \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: def:nt_limit

nodes.name: Boundary value
nodes.statement: The boundary value of $f$ at $\zeta$ is \[ f^*(\zeta)=\lim_{\mathcal{N}_\zeta}f, \] the limit along the nontangential filter $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$, read through the choice operator so that it is a total function. Where the nontangential limit at $\zeta$ exists, it equals $f^*(\zeta)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: def:boundary_function

nodes.name: The nontangential filter is nontrivial
nodes.statement: For $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb{D}$ and $\alpha>1$ the radial segment $[0,1)\zeta$ lies in $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$; hence $\mathcal{N}_\zeta\neq\bot$. \begin{proof} For $0\le r<1$ one has $|r\zeta|=r<1$ and $|\zeta-r\zeta|=1-r<\alpha(1-r)$. So $\zeta$ lies in the closure of $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$, making $\mathcal{N}_{\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)}(\zeta)$ nontrivial; a supremum of filters is nontrivial as soon as one of them is, so a single $\alpha$ suffices. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:nt_filter_neBot

nodes.name: Boundary values: pointwise, relational and canonical
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\partial\mathbb{D}$ carried by the circle. \begin{enumerate} \item If $f$ converges nontangentially at $\zeta$, then $f\to f^*(\zeta)$ along $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$. \item If $f$ has nontangential limit $L$ at $\zeta$, then $f^*(\zeta)=L$. \item If $g$ is an almost everywhere nontangential boundary value of $f$, then $g=f^*$ almost everywhere. \item Consequently $f^*$ is almost everywhere strongly measurable as soon as one such $g$ is. \end{enumerate} Part (3) is why measurability of a boundary function never needs a separate argument: it is inherited from whichever explicit representative the relevant existence theorem produces. \begin{proof} (1) is the choice of the canonical limit. For (2), uniqueness of limits uses the nontrivial filter $\mathcal{N}_\zeta$. Apply (2) almost everywhere for (3), and transfer measurability along that equality for (4). \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:boundary_value_bridge

nodes.name: Poisson kernel over a Stolz region
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha>1$. There is a constant $C_\alpha$ such that for every $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb{D}$, every $z\in\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$ and every $\theta$, \[ P_z(\theta)\ \le\ \frac{C_\alpha\,(1-|z|)}{\bigl((1-|z|)+|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|\bigr)^{2}} . \] In particular $P_z(\theta)\le C_\alpha/(1-|z|)$ always, and $P_z(\theta)\le C_\alpha (1-|z|)/|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|^{2}$ once $|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|\ge 2\alpha(1-|z|)$. Together with $\int P_z\,d\theta/2\pi=1$ this exhibits the Poisson kernels, restricted to a Stolz region, as an approximate identity with a uniformly integrable decreasing majorant. This single estimate replaces Garnett's Theorem I.4.2 and is the engine of both Lemma~\ref{lem:I_5_4} and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac}. \begin{proof} From $|e^{i\theta}-z|\ge 1-|z|$ and, by the triangle inequality and the definition of $\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$, $|e^{i\theta}-z|\ge|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|-\alpha(1-|z|)$, one gets $|e^{i\theta}-z|\ge c_\alpha\bigl((1-|z|)+|e^{i\theta}-\zeta|\bigr)$; insert this into $P_z(\theta)=(1-|z|^2)/|e^{i\theta}-z|^{2}$ and use $1-|z|^2\le 2(1-|z|)$. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:poisson_stolz_bound

nodes.name: Differentiation of measures on the circle
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:circle_differentiation

nodes.name: Uniform ball-density bound for positive Poisson integrals
nodes.statement:
Let $
u$ be a finite positive measure carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$, let $\|\zeta\|=1$, and suppose that for every $r>0$, \[ 
u(\overline B(\zeta,r)) \le c\,\sigma(\overline B(\zeta,r)). \] Then for $z\in\Gamma_\alpha(\zeta)$, \[ \int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}P_z\,d
u\le 8(\alpha+2)^2c. \]  egin{proof} Decompose the circle into dyadic chordal annuli centred at $\zeta$: with $\delta=1-|z|$, put $S_0=\overline B(\zeta,\delta)$ and $S_j=\overline B(\zeta,2^j\delta)\setminus\overline B(\zeta,2^{j-1}\delta)$. On $S_j$ the Stolz-region kernel bound gives $P_z\le 4A/(4^j\delta)$ with $A=2(\alpha+2)^2$, while the density hypothesis and the chord--arc estimate give $
u(S_j)\le c\,2^j\delta/2$; the product is $2Ac\,2^{-j}$ and $\sum_j 2^{-j}=2$, so the total is $4Ac=8(\alpha+2)^2c$, exactly the stated constant. In Lean the estimate is carried out for the lower integral, so that no piecewise integrability is needed, and transferred at the end by 	exttt{integral\_eq\_lintegral\_of\_nonneg\_ae}. Using 	exttt{lintegral\_iUnion\_le} rather than 	exttt{lintegral\_iUnion} means only that the annuli cover the plane has to be proved, not that they are pairwise disjoint. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:poisson_ball_density_bound

nodes.name: Density-zero Poisson integrals
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:poisson_density_zero

nodes.name: Garnett I.5.4: singular Poisson integrals vanish at the boundary
nodes.statement:
\mainline  ookref{Garnett}{I.5.4}{Chapter I, Section 5, PDF pages 41--42} If $
u$ is a finite signed measure on $\partial\mathbb{D}$ that is singular with respect to $d	heta$, then \[ \operatorname{nt}\lim_{z	o\zeta}P[
u](z)=0 \] for almost every $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb{D}$. This is the step that removes the singular part in Theorem~ef{thm:I_5_3}, and it is also what gives the singular functions of Definition~ef{def:singular_function_formula} boundary modulus one almost everywhere.  egin{proof} Mutual singularity makes the total variation of $
u$ singular with respect to $\sigma$. Expanding the Jordan decomposition and using subadditivity of vector-measure variation gives $\operatorname{var}(
u)\le |
u|$, so the variation measure is also carried by the circle and singular to $\sigma$. Theorem~ef{thm:circle_differentiation} gives density zero almost everywhere, and Lemma~ef{lem:poisson_density_zero} gives $P[\operatorname{var}(
u)]	o0$. Finally $|P[
u]|\le P[\operatorname{var}(
u)]$ follows from the vector-integral norm inequality, and squeezing proves the claim. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: lem:I_5_4

nodes.name: Fatou at Lebesgue points
nodes.statement: Let $k\in L^1(d\theta/2\pi)$. Then at every Lebesgue point $\zeta$ of $k$, and hence almost everywhere, \[ \operatorname{nt}\lim_{z\to\zeta}P\bigl[k\,d\theta/2\pi\bigr](z)=k(\zeta). \] \begin{proof} At a Lebesgue point put $d\rho_\zeta=|k-k(\zeta)|\,d\sigma$. Its ball-density quotient is exactly the mean oscillation of $k$, hence tends to zero. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson_density_zero} to $\rho_\zeta$, use $\int P_z\,d\sigma=1$, and bound $|P[k](z)-k(\zeta)|$ by $P[\rho_\zeta](z)$. The almost-everywhere statement follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_differentiation}. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:I_5_3_ac

nodes.name: Garnett I.5.3: Fatou theorem, $p=1$ disc form
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.5.3}{Chapter I, Section 5, PDF pages 40--41} Let $\mu$ be a finite signed measure on $\partial\mathbb{D}$, with Lebesgue decomposition $d\mu=k\,d\theta/2\pi+d\mu_s$, $\mu_s\perp d\theta$. Then the Poisson integral of $\mu$ has a nontangential limit at almost every boundary point, and \[ \operatorname{nt}\lim_{z\to\zeta}P[\mu](z)=k(\zeta) \qquad\text{for almost every }\zeta\in\partial\mathbb{D}; \] equivalently $\bigl(P[\mu]\bigr)^*=k$ almost everywhere, so the boundary function is in $L^1$. Garnett states the stronger half-plane theorem for all $1\le p\le\infty$; only this $p=1$ disc form is used in this project. \begin{proof} Split $\mu$ by the Lebesgue decomposition, which mathlib provides as \texttt{MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.singularPart\_add\_withDensity\_rnDeriv\_eq}, and add Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} to Lemma~\ref{lem:I_5_4}, using that nontangential limits are limits along a filter and therefore additive. The density part is identified with its signed Poisson integral by Lemma~\ref{lem:poisson_integral_linear}; integrability of the kernel against both summands then identifies their sum with $P[\mu]$. Finally use Lemma~\ref{lem:boundary_value_bridge} for the canonical boundary function. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.1 Chapter I: Poisson integrals and boundary values
nodes.label: thm:I_5_3

nodes.name: Garnett I.(3.5): Poisson integrals contract $L^p$, disc form
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{I.(3.5)}{Chapter I, Section 3, printed pages 14--15, PDF pages 26--27} Let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\sigma$ be normalized arclength on $\partial\mathbb{D}$, and let $U\in L^p(\sigma)$. Then for $0<r<1$, \[ \|P[U\,d\sigma](r\,\cdot)\|_{L^p(\sigma)}\le\|U\|_{L^p(\sigma)}, \] hence $\sup_{0<r<1}\|P[U\,d\sigma](r\,\cdot)\|_{L^p(\sigma)} \le\|U\|_{L^p(\sigma)}$. \begin{proof} For $p=\infty$ use $P_z\ge0$ and $\int P_z\,d\sigma=1$. For $1\le p<\infty$, Jensen's inequality for the probability measure $P_z\,d\sigma$ gives $|P[U\,d\sigma](z)|^p\le\int P_z|U|^p\,d\sigma$. Integrate over $z=r\eta$, exchange the integrals, and use $P_{r\eta}(\zeta)=P_{r\zeta}(\eta)$ for $|\eta|=|\zeta|=1$ together with total mass one. Garnett uses Minkowski's integral inequality instead, which mathlib lacks. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.2 Chapter I: harmonic representation
nodes.label: eq:I_3_5

nodes.name: $L^p$ dual representation
nodes.statement: \bookref{Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis}{6.16}{Real-valued case; the exponents $p$ and $q$ are interchanged relative to Rudin's notation} Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure and let $p,q$ be conjugate exponents with $1\le q<\infty$. For every bounded real linear functional $\Lambda$ on $L^q(\mu;\mathbb R)$, there exists a unique $U\in L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ such that \[ \|U\|_p=\|\Lambda\|, \qquad \Lambda(f)=\int Uf\,d\mu\quad(f\in L^q(\mu;\mathbb R)). \] \begin{proof} The pairing operator-norm bounds and uniqueness are proved. Existence remains unproved. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.2 Chapter I: harmonic representation
nodes.label: thm:lp_duality

nodes.name: Garnett I.3.5(a): bounded radial $L^p$ norms, disc form
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{I.3.5(a)}{Chapter I, Section 3, printed pages 17--19, PDF pages 29--31} Let $1<p\le\infty$, and let $\sigma$ be normalized arclength on $\partial\mathbb{D}$. A function $u:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R$ is harmonic on $\mathbb{D}$ and satisfies \[ \sup_{0<r<1}\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_{L^p(\sigma)}<\infty \] if and only if there exists $U\in L^p(\sigma)$ such that $u=P[U\,d\sigma]$ on $\mathbb{D}$. \begin{proof} On the unit disc put $u_t(\zeta)=u(t\zeta)$. The reproducing formula gives $u(tz)=\int P_z u_t\,d\sigma$. The uniformly bounded family $u_t\in L^p=(L^q)^*$, where $1/p+1/q=1$, has a weak-star cluster point $U$ as $t\to1$. Testing against the fixed kernel $P_z\in L^q$ gives $u=P[U\,d\sigma]$. Conversely, the Poisson operators are contractions on $L^p$ (Lemma~\ref{eq:I_3_5}). The Lean proof is complete relative to the finite-measure dual representation theorem in Theorem~\ref{thm:lp_duality}, whose existence proof remains open. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.2 Chapter I: harmonic representation
nodes.label: thm:I_3_5(a)

nodes.name: Garnett I.3.5(b): bounded radial $L^1$ means, disc form
nodes.statement:
ookref{Garnett}{I.3.5(b)}{Printed pages 17--18, PDF pages 29--30} A real harmonic function $u$ on $\mathbb{D}$ satisfies \[ \sup_{0<r<1}\int|u(r\zeta)|\,d\sigma(\zeta)<\infty \] if and only if $u=P[
u]$ for a finite signed measure on $\partial\mathbb{D}$.  egin{proof} The measures $d
u_r=u(r\zeta)\,d\sigma$ have uniformly bounded total variation. Take a weak-star cluster point $
u$ as $r\uparrow1$. In the reproducing identity $u(rz)=\int P_z\,d
u_r$, test against the fixed continuous kernel $P_z$ and use continuity of $u$ to get $u=P[
u]$. Conversely, positivity and unit mass of the kernel bound the radial $L^1$ means by the total variation of $
u$. Both linked proofs are open. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.2 Chapter I: harmonic representation
nodes.label: thm:I_3_5(b)

nodes.name: Garnett I.3.5(c): nonnegative harmonic representation, disc form
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.3.5(c)}{Printed pages 18--19, PDF pages 30--31} A real function $u$ on $\mathbb{D}$ is harmonic and nonnegative if and only if $u=P[\mu]$ for a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$. The measure has total mass $u(0)$. \begin{proof} Use the weak-star construction in the proof of I.3.5(b), as Garnett does: the approximating measures $u(r\zeta)\,d\sigma$ are positive and have common mass $u(0)$ by the mean-value property. Their cluster measure is therefore positive. The converse is positivity and harmonicity of the Poisson integral, already formalized; existence is open. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.2 Chapter I: harmonic representation
nodes.label: thm:I_3_5(c)

nodes.name: Harmonic mean-value characterization
nodes.statement: A continuous real function on an open subset of $\mathbb C$ is harmonic if and only if its average on every sufficiently small ball about each point equals its value at that point. A harmonic function has this property on every ball whose closure is contained in the domain. \begin{proof} The forward mean-value property and its local converse are both stated in Lean; their proofs remain open. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: thm:harmonic_mean_value

nodes.name: Garnett I.6.3: harmonic comparison characterization
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{I.6.3}{Printed pages 34--35, PDF pages 46--47} An upper semicontinuous $v:\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$ is subharmonic if and only if, for every bounded open $W$ compactly contained in $\Omega$ and every harmonic $u$ on $W$, the boundary condition $\limsup_{W\ni z\to\zeta}(v(z)-u(z))\le0$ implies $v\le u$ on $W$. \begin{proof} Apply the maximum principle to $v-u$. Conversely, approximate the upper semicontinuous boundary data from above by continuous functions, solve the Dirichlet problems, and pass to the circular mean inequality; integrating in the radius gives the ball mean inequality. The active Lean definition uses comparison on balls; the equivalence with the book's mean-value definition remains to be formalized. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: thm:I_6_3

nodes.name: Logarithm of modulus is subharmonic
nodes.statement: If $f$ is analytic on an open subset of $\mathbb{C}$, then $z\mapsto \log \lVert f(z)\rVert$, interpreted as $-\infty$ at zeros, is subharmonic there. This has been formalized both for complex-valued functions and, more generally, for functions taking values in a complex Banach space. Since the maximum of two subharmonic functions is subharmonic, so is $\log^+\lVert f\rVert=\max(\log\lVert f\rVert,0)$. \begin{proof} The Lean proofs are complete in the declarations linked above. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: thm:log_abs_subharmonic

nodes.name: Garnett I.6.4: integrability on interior circles
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{I.6.4}{Printed page 35, PDF page 47} If $v$ is subharmonic on a connected open set $\Omega$ and $v\not\equiv-\infty$, then its restriction to every circle bounding a closed disc in $\Omega$ is integrable and has finite mean. \begin{proof} Continuous boundary majorants and the positive Poisson kernel show that a circle mean of $-\infty$ would force $v=-\infty$ throughout its disc. The set where $v$ is locally $-\infty$ is then open and closed, contrary to connectedness and the hypothesis. Upper semicontinuity bounds the positive part on the circle. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: cor:I_6_4

nodes.name: Garnett I.6.5: Poisson modification
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{I.6.5}{Printed pages 35--36, PDF pages 47--48} For subharmonic $v\not\equiv-\infty$ on $\mathbb{D}$ and $0<r<1$, replace $v$ on $|z|<r$ by the Poisson integral of its values on $|z|=r$, leaving it unchanged outside. The resulting $v_r$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb{D}$, finite and harmonic on $|z|<r$, dominates $v$, and increases with $r$. \begin{proof} Circle integrability gives a finite harmonic extension. Approximate the boundary data from above and use harmonic comparison to obtain $v\le v_r$. The approximate-identity estimate gives upper semicontinuity across $|z|=r$, and the mean inequality gives subharmonicity there. Comparing successive modifications gives monotonicity. These four properties are stated in Lean but their proofs remain open. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: thm:I_6_5

nodes.name: Harnack's inequality on a disc
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be harmonic on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\mathbb{D}}(c,R)$ and nonnegative on $\partial\mathbb{D}(c,R)$. Then for $w$ with $\rho=|w-c|<R$, \[ \frac{R-\rho}{R+\rho}\,u(c)\ \le\ u(w)\ \le\ \frac{R+\rho}{R-\rho}\,u(c). \] The two-sided kernel estimate $\frac{R-\rho}{R+\rho}\le P_w(\zeta)\le\frac{R+\rho}{R-\rho}$ underlying it is recorded separately, since it is used on its own. \begin{proof} The kernel bounds come from mathlib's estimates on the real part of the Herglotz--Riesz kernel. Insert them into the Poisson integral formula $u(w)=\int P_w u\,d\sigma$, using $u\ge0$ on the circle to preserve the inequalities, and identify $\int u\,d\sigma$ with $u(c)$ by the mean value property. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: lem:harnack_inequality

nodes.name: Harnack's convergence theorem
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{I.6.7, proof}{Invoked on printed page 37, PDF page 49} Let $u_n$ be an increasing sequence of real harmonic functions on a connected domain. If $\sup_n u_n(z_0)<\infty$ at one interior point, then $u_n$ converges locally uniformly to a finite harmonic function. \begin{proof} Apply Harnack's inequality to the nonnegative differences $u_m-u_n$; convergence at one point gives uniform Cauchy estimates on compact subsets by a chain of discs. Pass the mean-value identity to the local uniform limit. For Poisson modifications, apply this on each smaller disc to a cofinal sequence of radii. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: thm:harnack_convergence

nodes.name: Harmonic majorants of subharmonic functions, Garnett I.6.7
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{I.6.7}{Chapter I, Section 6, printed pages 36--37, PDF pages 48--49} Let $v$ be subharmonic on $\mathbb{D}$. Then $v$ has a harmonic majorant on $\mathbb{D}$ if and only if \[ \sup_{0<r<1}\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}v(r e^{i\theta})\,d\theta = \sup_{0<r<1} v_r(0) < \infty, \] where $v_r$ is the Poisson extension to $|z|<r$ of the boundary values of $v$ on $|z|=r$. When this condition holds and $v\not\equiv-\infty$, the least harmonic majorant $u$ of $v$ is given by \[ u(z)=\lim_{r\to 1} \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} P_{z/r}(\theta)v(r e^{i\theta})\,d\theta =\lim_{r\to 1}v_r(z). \] \begin{proof} The modifications $v_r$ increase and are harmonic on expanding discs. If their values at zero are bounded, Harnack's convergence theorem gives a finite harmonic limit $u\ge v$. Every harmonic majorant $U$ dominates every $v_r$ by comparison, hence dominates $u$; this proves leastness. Conversely $v_r\le U$ bounds their values at zero. The case $v\equiv-\infty$ has harmonic majorants but no least one and is excluded from the second assertion. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.3 Chapter I: subharmonic functions and harmonic majorants
nodes.label: thm:I_6_7

nodes.name: Multiplicity and the Blaschke sum
nodes.statement: For $m:\mathbb C\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$, define \[ \mathcal B(m)=\sum_{a\in\mathbb D}m(a)(1-|a|)\in[0,+\infty]. \] An analytic function uses $m_f(a)=\operatorname{ord}_a(f)$; a family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ uses $m(a)=\#\{i\in I:a_i=a\}$, with infinite cardinalities recorded as $\infty$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: def:blaschke_sum

nodes.name: Blaschke condition for a multiplicity function
nodes.statement: A multiplicity function $m$ satisfies Blaschke's condition on $\mathbb D$ if $\mathcal B(m)<\infty$. In that case $m(a)<\infty$ for every $a\in\mathbb D$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: def:blaschke_condition

nodes.name: Lean Blaschke factors
nodes.statement: For $R>0$ and $|a|<R$, the elementary Blaschke factor is \[ b_{R,a}(z)=\frac{R(z-a)}{R^2-\overline a z}. \] Its normalized form is $b_{R,0}$ when $a=0$, and $-\overline a\,b_{R,a}/|a|$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: def:blaschke_factor

nodes.name: Blaschke product of a multiplicity function
nodes.statement: For $m:\mathbb C\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$, with $b_a$ the normalized factor $b_{1,a}$, \[ B_m(z)=z^{m(0)}\prod_{a\in\mathbb{D}\setminus\{0\}}b_a(z)^{m(a)}, \] the product taken unconditionally, i.e.\ as the limit along finite subsets of $\mathbb{D}$. An analytic function uses $m=\operatorname{ord}(f)$ and a finite or infinite family $(a_i)$ uses $m(a)=\#\{i:a_i=a\}$. Points outside $\mathbb{D}$ are ignored.
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: def:blaschke_product

nodes.name: Garnett II.2.1: the Blaschke condition
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.2.1}{Chapter II, Section 2, PDF pages 63--64} If $f$ is a nonzero analytic function on $\mathbb D$ and $\log|f|$ has a harmonic majorant, then $\mathcal B(m_f)<\infty$. If moreover $f(0)\ne0$ and $u$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$, then \[ \mathcal B(m_f)\le u(0)-\log|f(0)|. \] \begin{proof} Jensen's formula and the harmonic mean-value property bound the logarithmic zero sums. Let the radius tend to one and use $1-|a|\le-\log|a|$ to obtain the quantitative bound. For the general case, remove the finite-order zero at the origin, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} to obtain a least harmonic majorant, and then restore the origin zero. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: thm:II_2_1

nodes.name: Garnett II.2.2: convergence and boundary size of Blaschke products
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.2.2}{Chapter II, Section 2, PDF page 64} If $m$ satisfies the Blaschke condition, then the finite partial products of $B_m$ converge uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb{D}$ to a bounded analytic function whose zeros are exactly the points with $m(w)>0$, with the prescribed multiplicities, and whose boundary modulus is one almost everywhere. More precisely, $|B_m|\le1$ on $\mathbb{D}$ and $\operatorname{ord}_w B_m=m(w)$ for every $w\in\mathbb{D}$. Its extension by zero outside $\mathbb{D}$ belongs to $H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$. Almost everywhere on the circle, its canonical boundary value is its nontangential limit and has modulus one. \begin{proof} The passage from the product omitting origin zeros to the full product $B(z)=z^mP(z)$ is formalized: multiplication by $z^m$, whose modulus is at most one on $\mathbb{D}$, preserves locally uniform convergence. Analyticity of $B$ is formalized from this convergence: the finite products are holomorphic since $|\overline{a}z|<1$ for $a,z\in\mathbb{D}$, and a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic. The bound $|B|\le1$ is formalized by bounding each finite product and passing to the pointwise limit. The factor bound follows from $|1-\overline a z|^2-|z-a|^2=(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)\ge0$. Membership in $H^\infty$ follows from analyticity and $|B|\le1$, and the zero set is read off from the multiplicity formula, since an analytic function vanishes exactly where its order is nonzero. Convergence of the product omitting origin zeros, the multiplicity formula, and the boundary modulus remain to be proved. For the boundary modulus, first remove the origin zeros and let $B_n$ be the finite partial products. The tail product $Q_n=B/B_n$ is bounded analytic. Corollary~\ref{cor:II_3_2(p=∞)} gives \[ |Q_n(0)|\le\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}|Q_n^*|\,d\sigma =\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}|B^*|\,d\sigma\le1. \] Here $|B_n|=1$ on the circle and $|Q_n(0)|\to1$, so $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere. Restoring the origin factor preserves the boundary modulus. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: thm:II_2_2

nodes.name: Garnett II.2.4: radial means and least harmonic majorants
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.2.4}{Chapter II, Section 2, PDF page 66} Let $f$ be analytic on $\mathbb D$ with $|f|\le1$. Consider: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $f=\lambda B$, where $|\lambda|=1$ and $B$ is a Blaschke product; \item[(b)] \[ \lim_{r\uparrow1}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} \log|f(r e^{i\theta})|\,d\theta=0; \] \item[(c)] the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$ is the zero function. \end{enumerate} We formalize $(a)\Rightarrow(b)$ and $(b)\Leftrightarrow(c)$, which suffice for Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}. The logarithm and its radial means take values in $\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$, with $\log0=-\infty$. \begin{proof} For $(a)\Rightarrow(b)$, remove a finite initial Blaschke product so that the remaining product has modulus at the origin arbitrarily close to one; apply the subharmonic mean inequality and let the radius tend to one. For $(b)\Leftrightarrow(c)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} identifies the radial limit with $u(0)$ for the least harmonic majorant $u\le0$. The harmonic maximum principle gives $u(0)=0$ if and only if $u\equiv0$. This equivalence is formalized using the existing prerequisite theorems; the proof of $(a)\Rightarrow(b)$ remains to be formalized. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.4 Chapter II, Section 2: Blaschke products
nodes.label: thm:II_2_4

nodes.name: II.3.1, $p=\infty$: boundary values on the disc
nodes.statement: This is the $p=\infty$ endpoint analogue of the boundary-limit conclusion of Garnett II.3.1 on the disc (Chapter II, Section 3, PDF page 67); the numbered theorem itself is stated for $0<p<\infty$. Every bounded analytic function on $\mathbb{D}$, in particular every $f\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$, has a finite nontangential limit at almost every boundary point. \begin{proof} The real and imaginary parts of $f$ are bounded harmonic, hence Poisson integrals of $L^\infty$ boundary data by Theorem~\ref{thm:I_3_5(a)} with $p=\infty$. These densities lie in $L^1$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} gives their nontangential limits almost everywhere. Intersect the two full-measure sets and combine the real and imaginary limits. The $H^\infty$ case uses the equality of the Hardy norm with the pointwise supremum. Both Lean proofs are complete; I.3.5(a) remains an unproved prerequisite. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values
nodes.label: cor:II_3_1(p=∞)

nodes.name: Garnett II.3.2, $p=\infty$: Poisson representation on the disc
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.3.2 ($p=\infty$)}{Chapter II, Section 3, printed page 56, PDF page 68; disc form} Let $\sigma$ be normalized arclength on $\partial\mathbb{D}$ and let $U\in L^\infty(\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Then $U$ is the a.e. nontangential boundary value of an $H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ function if and only if $P[U\,d\sigma]$ is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$. Every such function equals $P[U\,d\sigma]$ on $\mathbb{D}$. In particular, for $f\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$, \[ f(z)=P[f^*\,d\sigma](z),\qquad |f(0)|\le\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}|f^*|\,d\sigma. \] \begin{proof} Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_3_5(a)} to the real and imaginary parts of a bounded analytic function. Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} identifies the resulting densities with its boundary values. Conversely, positivity and unit mass of the Poisson kernel give the $L^\infty$ bound, and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3_ac} gives the prescribed boundary values. At the origin the kernel is one, giving the displayed inequality. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.5 Chapter II, Section 3: bounded analytic boundary values
nodes.label: cor:II_3_2(p=∞)

nodes.name: Garnett II.4.1: logarithmic inequality, $H^\infty$ disc case
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.4.1 ($p=\infty$)}{Printed page 62, PDF page 74} If $f\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ is not identically zero, then $\log|f^*|\in L^1(\sigma)$, with $\log0=-\infty$, and \[ \log|f(z)|\le P[\log|f^*|\,d\sigma](z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb{D}). \] \begin{proof} Follow Garnett's proof: apply I.6.7 to $\log|f|$, use dominated convergence for the positive logarithmic parts and Fatou's lemma for the negative parts, then remove a possible zero at the origin. In the bounded case a constant dominates the positive parts. This is the case used below; the full $0<p<\infty$ theorem additionally uses the integrable maximal function of II.3.1 and is not asserted here. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: thm:II_4_1

nodes.name: Garnett II.4.2: boundary uniqueness, $H^\infty$ disc case
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.4.2 ($p=\infty$)}{Printed page 62, PDF page 74} If $f\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ and its boundary value vanishes on a set of positive arclength measure, then $f\equiv0$. Equivalently, every nonzero bounded analytic function has nonzero boundary values almost everywhere. \begin{proof} For nonzero $f$, II.4.1 makes the extended boundary logarithm integrable, whereas it is $-\infty$ wherever $f^*=0$. Thus that set has measure zero. This result precedes and is used by II.5.3; it is not derived from it. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: cor:II_4_2

nodes.name: Outer functions on the disc
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.4, II.5}{Printed pages 64 and 70, PDF pages 76 and 82} For real $k\in L^1(\sigma)$, where $\sigma$ is normalized arclength on $\partial\mathbb{D}$, put \[ O_k(z)=\exp\left(\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}} \frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,k(\zeta)\,d\sigma(\zeta)\right). \] A function $f$ is outer on $\mathbb{D}$ if $f=C O_k$ on $\mathbb{D}$ for some such $k$ and a constant $|C|=1$.
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: def:outer_factor

nodes.name: Basic properties of outer functions
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.4, II.5}{Printed pages 64 and 70, PDF pages 76 and 82} For real $k\in L^1(\sigma)$, $O_k$ is analytic and zero-free on $\mathbb{D}$, and $\log|O_k|=P[k\,d\sigma]$ on $\mathbb{D}$. Hence every outer function $F$ is analytic and zero-free on $\mathbb{D}$, $\log|F|=P[k\,d\sigma]$ for some real $k\in L^1(\sigma)$. \begin{proof} The integral $\int\frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,k(\zeta)\,d\sigma(\zeta)$ is analytic in $z\in\mathbb{D}$, and its real part is $P[k\,d\sigma](z)$ because the real part of the Herglotz--Riesz kernel is the Poisson kernel. Exponentiating gives the claims for $O_k$; multiplying by $|C|=1$ gives those for $F$. No Nevanlinna boundary theorem is used here. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: thm:outer_function_properties

nodes.name: Garnett II.4.4: prescribed bounded boundary modulus, disc form
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.4.4 ($p=\infty$)}{Printed page 63, PDF page 75} Let $h\ge0$ be essentially bounded and not zero almost everywhere on $\partial\mathbb{D}$. There is a nonzero $f\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ with $|f^*|=h$ almost everywhere if and only if $\log h\in L^1(\sigma)$, where $\log0=-\infty$. When this holds, the normalized outer function $O_{\log h}$ has the required modulus and satisfies $|O_{\log h}(z)|\le\|h\|_\infty$. \begin{proof} Necessity is II.4.1. For sufficiency use Garnett's construction $\exp(u+iv)$, where $u=P[\log h\,d\sigma]$ and $v$ is its normalized harmonic conjugate. The bound $u\le\log\|h\|_\infty$ gives boundedness. Bounded-analytic Fatou gives complex boundary limits, and Poisson Fatou identifies their moduli with $h$. The finite-$p$ refinement in the book is not needed for the factorization roadmap. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: thm:II_4_4

nodes.name: Boundary modulus of an outer function
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.4, outer boundary modulus}{Printed page 64, PDF page 76} For real $k\in L^1(\sigma)$, $O_k$ has finite nontangential limits almost everywhere and $|O_k^*|=e^k$ almost everywhere. \begin{proof} The book's outer construction permits arbitrary integrable logarithmic data. To justify finite complex boundary limits without II.5.3, write $k=k^+-k^-$ and $O_k=O_{-k^-}/O_{-k^+}$. Apply the bounded construction II.4.4 to $e^{-k^-}$ and $e^{-k^+}$; their boundary moduli are positive almost everywhere. Taking the quotient gives modulus $e^k$. This supplies the disc-form detail behind the boundary assertion after the outer definition, independently of Nevanlinna boundary theory. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: thm:outer_boundary_modulus

nodes.name: Outer uniqueness
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.4, outer uniqueness}{Printed page 64, PDF page 76} If two outer functions $F_1,F_2$ satisfy $|F_1^*|=|F_2^*|$ almost everywhere on $\partial\mathbb{D}$, then $F_1=cF_2$ on $\mathbb{D}$ for a constant $|c|=1$. \begin{proof} Write $F_j=C_jO_{k_j}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:outer_boundary_modulus}, $e^{k_1}=|F_1^*|=|F_2^*|=e^{k_2}$ almost everywhere, so $k_1=k_2$ almost everywhere and $\log|F_1|=P[k_1\,d\sigma]=\log|F_2|$ on $\mathbb{D}$. The quotient $F_1/F_2$ is analytic with modulus one, hence a unimodular constant by the maximum modulus principle. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.6 Chapter II, Section 4: logarithmic integrability and outer functions
nodes.label: thm:outer_uniqueness

nodes.name: Nevanlinna class
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.1)}{Chapter II, Section 5, printed page 66, PDF page 78} The Nevanlinna class $N$ consists of analytic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ such that \[ \sup_{0<r<1}\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}\log^+|f(r\zeta)|\,d\sigma(\zeta)<\infty, \] where $\sigma$ is normalized arclength. In Lean, functions are extended by zero outside $\mathbb{D}$. \emph{Equivalent definition (Garnett (5.1)).} An analytic function $f$ belongs to $N$ if and only if $\log^+|f|$ has a harmonic majorant on $\mathbb{D}$. \begin{proof} For the equivalence, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} to the subharmonic function $\log^+|f|=\max(\log|f|,0)$. Conversely, a harmonic majorant $U\ge\log^+|f|\ge0$ bounds every radial $\log^+$ mean by $U(0)$, by the mean-value property. These dependencies concern the equivalence; the radial-integral definition itself needs neither result. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures
nodes.label: def:Nevanlinna_class

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.1: harmonic-majorant characterization of $N$
nodes.statement:
\mainline  ookref{Garnett}{II.5.1}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 78} Let $f$ be analytic on $\mathbb{D}$, $f
ot\equiv0$. Then $f\in N$ if and only if the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$ is $P[\mu]$ for a finite signed measure $\mu$ on $\partial\mathbb{D}$. Equivalently, $\log|f|$ admits a majorant $P[
u]$ for some finite signed boundary measure $
u$.  egin{proof} If $f\in N$, take a nonnegative harmonic majorant $U$ of $\log^+|f|$ and let $u\le U$ be the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$, which exists since $f
ot\equiv0$. Apply Theorem~ef{thm:I_3_5(c)} to $U$ and $U-u$ and subtract their representing measures to obtain $u=P[\mu]$. Conversely, the Jordan identity (Lemma~ef{lem:poisson_integral_linear}) gives, even if $P[\mu]$ is only a majorant rather than the least one, $\log^+|f|\le P[\mu^+]$, a nonnegative harmonic majorant; hence $f\in N$ by the equivalent definition in Definition~ef{def:Nevanlinna_class}. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures
nodes.label: thm:II_5_1

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.2: remove the zeros of a Nevanlinna function
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.2}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 78} Let $f\in N$ be nonzero and let $B$ be the Blaschke product formed from the zeros of $f$, counted with multiplicity. Then $B$ converges and $f=Bg$, where the quotient $g=f/B$, with its removable singularities filled in, is analytic and zero-free on $\mathbb{D}$, and $g$ still belongs to the Nevanlinna class. Moreover, $\log|g|$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$ on $\mathbb{D}$. \begin{proof} By (5.1), $\log|f|\le\log^+|f|\le U$ for a harmonic $U$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_1} gives the Blaschke condition, and Theorem~\ref{thm:I_6_7} gives the least harmonic majorant $u\le U$ of $\log|f|$. Since $B$ has the zeros of $f$ with the same multiplicities (Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_2}), $f/B$ has only removable singularities; removing them gives a zero-free analytic $g$ with $f=Bg$. As $|B|\le1$, $\log|g|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$, so $u\le\log|g|$. Conversely, $u-\log|g|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log|B|$, whose least harmonic majorant is $0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_4}; hence $u=\log|g|$. Finally $\log^+|g|=\max(u,0)\le U$, so $g\in N$ by (5.1). \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures
nodes.label: lem:II_5_2

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.3: boundary values and the least-majorant measure
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.3}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 79} Let $f\in N$, $f\not\equiv0$. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item $f$ has a nontangential limit $f^*(\zeta)$ at almost every $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb{D}$, and $f^*\ne0$ almost everywhere; \item $\log|f^*|\in L^1(d\theta/2\pi)$; \item the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$ is $P[\mu]$ for a finite signed measure $\mu$ on $\partial\mathbb{D}$, unique by Theorem~\ref{thm:poisson_measure_unique}, and \begin{equation} d\mu=\log|f^*|\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}+d\mu_s, \qquad \mu_s\perp d\theta . \end{equation} \end{enumerate} In other words, the absolutely continuous part of the representing measure is exactly the boundary logarithm, and the whole obstruction to the inequality $\log|f(z)|\le\int\log|f^*|P_z\,d\theta/2\pi$ is concentrated in the singular part; Garnett's class $N^+$ is the subclass where $\mu_s\le0$. \begin{proof} Let $B$ be the Blaschke product over the zeros of $f$ and $g=f/B$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:II_5_1} and Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}, $g$ is zero-free and $\log|g|=P[\mu]$ is the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:poisson_measure_unique} the measure $\mu$ is unique. Write $d\mu=k\,d\theta/2\pi+d\mu_s$ using mathlib's Lebesgue decomposition for signed measures. By Theorem~\ref{thm:I_5_3}, $\log|g|$ has nontangential limit $k$ almost everywhere, and since $|B^*|=1$ almost everywhere (Theorem~\ref{thm:II_2_2}) the same holds for $\log|f|$. So $k\in L^1$ and \eqref{eq:II_5_3_decomposition} follow once $f$ itself is known to have nontangential limits. For that, decompose $\log|g|=u_1-u_2$ with $u_j=P[\mu_j]\ge0$ harmonic, $\mu=\mu_1-\mu_2$ the Jordan decomposition. Choose harmonic conjugates $v_j$ with $v_j(0)=0$, which exist because the disc is simply connected and which mathlib provides as \texttt{InnerProductSpace.HarmonicOnNhd.exists\_analyticOnNhd\_ball\_re\_eq}; then $\log g=(u_1+iv_1)-(u_2+iv_2)+ic$ for a real constant $c$, so that \[ g=e^{ic}\,\frac{e^{-(u_2+iv_2)}}{e^{-(u_1+iv_1)}} . \] Each $e^{-(u_j+iv_j)}$ has modulus $e^{-u_j}\le1$, hence lies in $H^\infty$ and has nontangential limits almost everywhere by Corollary~\ref{cor:II_3_1(p=∞)}. Each exponential is nonzero on the disc, so II.4.2 makes its boundary limit nonzero almost everywhere. In particular the denominator has a nonzero boundary limit, and the displayed quotient gives the finite boundary limits of $g$, and then of $f=Bg$. Combining those limits with the finite limit of $\log|g|$ identifies $k=\log|f^*|$ and proves (5.2) and (5.3). \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.7 Chapter II, Section 5: Nevanlinna boundary measures
nodes.label: thm:II_5_3

nodes.name: Jordan decomposition of singular measures
nodes.statement:
ookref{Garnett}{II, (5.7)}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} Let $
u$ be a finite real signed measure with Jordan decomposition $
u=
u^+-
u^-$. Then $|
u|(S)=0$ if and only if $
u^+(S)=
u^-(S)=0$, and $
u\perp\sigma$ if and only if $
u^+\perp\sigma$ and $
u^-\perp\sigma$. In particular, if $
u$ is carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$ and singular with respect to Lebesgue measure, then $
u^+$ and $
u^-$ are finite positive measures with the same two properties. This decomposition is unique among differences of mutually singular positive measures (Jordan uniqueness).  egin{proof} The total variation is $|
u|=
u^++
u^-$, and a sum of positive measures vanishes on $S$, or is singular to $\sigma$, exactly when both summands do. Uniqueness is the injectivity of the signed measure associated with a Jordan decomposition, supplied by mathlib. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors
nodes.label: thm:jordan_decomposition_singular_measure

nodes.name: Singular function formula
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.8)}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} For a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$ and singular to normalized arclength $\sigma$, put \[ S_\mu(z)=\exp\left(-\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}} \frac{\zeta+z}{\zeta-z}\,d\mu(\zeta)\right). \] A function $S$ is singular on $\mathbb{D}$ if $S=S_\mu$ on $\mathbb{D}$ for some such $\mu$.
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors
nodes.label: def:singular_function_formula

nodes.name: Garnett II, (5.9): modulus of $S_\mu$
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.9)}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} For a finite positive measure $\mu$ carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$, $S_\mu$ is analytic and zero-free on $\mathbb{D}$, \[ \log|S_\mu(z)|=-P[\mu](z)\quad(z\in\mathbb{D}), \] and $S_\mu(0)=e^{-\mu(\partial\mathbb{D})}$. In particular $|S_\mu|\le1$ on $\mathbb{D}$. Every singular function is therefore analytic, zero-free and bounded by one on $\mathbb{D}$, has positive value at zero, and belongs to $H^\infty$ after extension by zero. \begin{proof} The Herglotz--Riesz transform of $\mu$ is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$, and its real part is $P[\mu]$ because the real part of the Herglotz--Riesz kernel is the Poisson kernel. At $z=0$ the kernel equals $1$ on $\partial\mathbb{D}$. Positivity of the Poisson kernel gives $P[\mu]\ge0$, hence $|S_\mu|\le1$. The representation defining a singular function transfers these properties to $S$; bounded analyticity gives membership in $H^\infty$. No boundary-limit theorem or converse characterization is used in these consequences. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors
nodes.label: eq:II_5_9

nodes.name: Characterization of singular functions
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.5}{Printed page 70, PDF page 82} A function $S$ is singular if and only if it is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$, has no zeros there, satisfies $|S|\le1$, has nontangential limits of modulus one $\sigma$-almost everywhere, and $S(0)$ is positive real. In particular every singular function belongs to $H^\infty$. \begin{proof} The exponential integral is analytic and satisfies $\log|S_\mu|=-P[\mu]$. Positivity, the singular Poisson boundary theorem, and bounded-analytic Fatou give the four properties. Conversely, represent the nonnegative harmonic function $-\log|S|$ as $P[\mu]$. Its zero boundary limit makes the absolutely continuous part of $\mu$ vanish. Then $S/S_\mu$ is a unimodular constant, equal to one by positivity at the origin. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.8 Chapter II, Section 5: singular factors
nodes.label: thm:singular_function_characterization

nodes.name: Algebraic structure of $N$
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II.5}{Chapter II, Section 5, printed page 66, PDF page 78} $N$ is closed under sums, scalar multiples, and products. If $f\in N$ has no zeros in $\mathbb{D}$, then $1/f\in N$; hence $f/g\in N$ whenever $f,g\in N$ and $g$ has no zeros in $\mathbb{D}$. Moreover $H^p\subseteq N$ for every $p>0$. \begin{proof} Sums, scalar multiples, and products follow from $\log^+|ab|\le\log^+|a|+\log^+|b|$ and $\log^+|a+b|\le\log^+|a|+\log^+|b|+\log2$. If $U$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|f|$ and $f$ has no zeros, then $U-\log|f|$ is a harmonic majorant of $\log^+|1/f|=\log^+|f|-\log|f|$, so $1/f\in N$ by (5.1). Finally $H^p\subseteq N$ because $\log^+x\le x^p/p$. \end{proof}
nodes.section: 1.9 Nevanlinna closure and outer membership
nodes.label: thm:nevanlinna_algebra

nodes.name: Outer functions belong to the Nevanlinna class
nodes.statement: Every outer function on $\mathbb{D}$ belongs to $N$ after extension by zero. \begin{proof} If $\log|F|=P[k\,d\sigma]$, positivity of the Poisson kernel gives $\log^+|F|\le P[k^+\,d\sigma]$, a nonnegative harmonic majorant. \end{proof}

nodes.label: thm:outer_mem_nevanlinna

nodes.name: Canonical factorization
nodes.statement: \bookref{Garnett}{II, (5.10)}{Printed page 71, PDF page 83} Let $|C|=1$, let $F$ be outer, and let $\mu_1,\mu_2$ be finite positive measures carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$, each singular to normalized arclength, with $\mu_1\perp\mu_2$. Then $(C,F,\mu_1,\mu_2)$ is a canonical factorization of $f$ if the zeros of $f$ in $\mathbb{D}$, counted with multiplicity, satisfy the Blaschke condition and, with $B$ their Blaschke product, \[ f = C\,B\,F\,S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}\quad\text{on }\mathbb{D}. \]
nodes.section: 1.10 Garnett II.5.5: canonical factorization
nodes.label: def:canonical_factorization

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.5: existence of canonical factorization in $N$
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.5 (existence)}{Chapter II, Section 5, PDF page 83} If $f\in N$ and $f\not\equiv0$, then $f$ has a canonical factorization $f=C\,B\,F\,S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}$ on $\mathbb{D}$.

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:II_5_2}, $f=Bg$ with $g\in N$ zero-free and $\log|g|$ the least harmonic majorant of $\log|f|$. By (5.2) and (5.3), that majorant is $P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$ with $k=\log|f^*|\in L^1(\sigma)$ and $\mu_s\perp\sigma$; least harmonic majorants are unique, so $\log|g|=P[k\,d\sigma+\mu_s]$ on $\mathbb{D}$. Put $\mu_2=\mu_s^+$ and $\mu_1=\mu_s^-$, which are carried by $\partial\mathbb{D}$, singular to $\sigma$, and mutually singular. By linearity of the Poisson integral and (5.9), $\log|g|=\log|O_k S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2}|$ on $\mathbb{D}$. Garnett concludes by taking a single-valued logarithm of the zero-free quotient $g$. We instead note that $g/(O_k S_{\mu_1}/S_{\mu_2})$ is analytic on $\mathbb{D}$ with modulus one, hence a unimodular constant $C$ by the maximum modulus principle. This is equivalent and avoids holomorphic logarithms on the disc.

nodes.name: Garnett II.5.5: converse
nodes.statement: \mainline \bookref{Garnett}{II.5.5 (converse)}{Printed page 71, PDF page 83} If $B$ is the Blaschke product of a multiplicity satisfying the Blaschke condition, $F$ is outer, $S_1,S_2$ are singular, and $C\in\mathbb C$, then $CBFS_1/S_2\in N$. The implemented algebraic proof permits arbitrary $C$; the book assumes $|C|=1$. \begin{proof} The convergence, analyticity and boundedness parts of II.2.2 give $B\in H^\infty\subseteq N$. Its multiplicity and boundary-modulus assertions are not used here. The elementary consequences of (5.9) give $S_1,S_2\in H^\infty\subseteq N$ and $S_2\ne0$ on $\mathbb{D}$, without using the full singular-function characterization. Also $F\in N$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:outer_mem_nevanlinna}. Closure of $N$ under reciprocals of zero-free functions gives $1/S_2\in N$. Multiplication and scalar multiplication then give $CBFS_1/S_2\in N$. In Lean each factor is extended by zero outside $\mathbb{D}$; the indicator of the product and quotient equals the corresponding product of indicators. This is the existing Lean proof. It differs from Garnett's direct signed Poisson-majorant argument: the equivalent definition in Definition~\ref{def:Nevanlinna_class} is used upstream for outer membership and reciprocal closure, but Theorem~\ref{thm:II_5_1} and its signed-measure representation are not invoked. \end{proof}
